title: Static routing: when it is still the right answer

videos.script: Lesson 14 read a routing table. This lesson writes one, by hand. {{table}} A static route is a line somebody typed. To reach this network, send the packet to that neighbour. There is no protocol, no message between routers, nothing to agree on. {{line}} On a large network that is a lot of typing, and nobody does it. On a small one, or on a branch with a single way out, it is still what most engineers choose. This lesson says why. {{small}} The lab is three routers in a row, with a computer at each end. A spare cable joins the first router to the last. {{chain}} You will add a route and watch a ping fail anyway, because the reply has no way home. Then you will add the way back and count the routers on the path. {{oneway}} After that comes a backup route and a pulled cable. That is where you meet the limit of the whole approach. A static route knows about its own router's cables, and nothing else. {{cable}} Last, the router at the far end swaps its routes for a single default. For a network with one exit, that is all it needs. {{stub}}
